title: AI flags Julie Knichel’s brain hemorrhage, and she returns to nursing after aneurysm treatment
summary: Software, apparently Viz.ai, detected Julie Knichel’s brain bleed and alerted her doctors; after treatment, she returned to full-time nursing.
account: Julie Knichel, a 57-year-old nurse, suffered a ruptured brain aneurysm. Her symptoms began on 2 February 2024. Baptist Health gives the day and month, and Jan Engoren’s subsequent interviews with Knichel and her surgeon, Brian Snelling, establish the year. At Baptist Health's Marcus Neuroscience Institute, software reviewed her scan and alerted clinicians to the bleeding. They sealed the aneurysm with coils delivered through a catheter. After about three weeks in the hospital, she recovered and returned to full-time nursing. On 29 October 2024, Snelling told CBS12 that the hospital's AI had picked up Knichel's bleeding before emergency doctors or radiologists had detected it. On 29 April 2025, The Coastal Star reported that Knichel had returned to full-time work with no lasting effects. That article does not mention AI. It credits her quick action in calling 911 and the medics who treated her. On 22 October 2025, NeurologyLive published an interview in which the surgeon names Viz.ai and describes an unnamed intensive care unit nurse whose circumstances match Knichel’s. The product attribution is therefore inferred. No account identifies the module or release.
purpose: Detect brain hemorrhage and alert clinicians.
system: Viz.ai stroke detection and care coordination (attribution inferred)

ratings.reason: Knichel survived a life-threatening hemorrhage and resumed her work and activities.

ai_role.statement: AI flagged the bleeding and notified the stroke team, according to her treating surgeon. Clinicians treated the aneurysm. Viz.ai is an inferred identification from his separate interview. The sources do not isolate the software’s effect on survival.

fields.summary: Software, apparently Viz.ai, detected Julie Knichel’s brain bleed and alerted her doctors; after treatment, she returned to full-time nursing.
fields.account: Julie Knichel, a 57-year-old nurse, suffered a ruptured brain aneurysm. Her symptoms began on 2 February 2024. Baptist Health gives the day and month, and Jan Engoren’s subsequent interviews with Knichel and her surgeon, Brian Snelling, establish the year. At Baptist Health's Marcus Neuroscience Institute, software reviewed her scan and alerted clinicians to the bleeding. They sealed the aneurysm with coils delivered through a catheter. After about three weeks in the hospital, she recovered and returned to full-time nursing. On 29 October 2024, Snelling told CBS12 that the hospital's AI had picked up Knichel's bleeding before emergency doctors or radiologists had detected it. On 29 April 2025, The Coastal Star reported that Knichel had returned to full-time work with no lasting effects. That article does not mention AI. It credits her quick action in calling 911 and the medics who treated her. On 22 October 2025, NeurologyLive published an interview in which the surgeon names Viz.ai and describes an unnamed intensive care unit nurse whose circumstances match Knichel’s. The product attribution is therefore inferred. No account identifies the module or release.
